passages.passage_text:
Every morning the sun has risen, and every morning we have inferred that it will rise again. David Hume's challenge to this ordinary habit of mind is easy to state and notoriously hard to dispel. Our confidence in the future, he argued, rests on the assumption that the future will resemble the past. But what grounds that assumption? It cannot be demonstrated by reasoning alone, since there is no contradiction in supposing that the course of nature might change tomorrow. And it cannot be established by experience without circularity, since the only experience we have is of past regularities, and to treat these as evidence about the future is precisely to assume the uniformity in question. The inference from observed to unobserved cases, on this view, is a habit of expectation produced by repetition, not a conclusion that reason has earned.

Responses to Hume have tended to divide into two camps. The first accepts that no justification of induction is available and tries to live comfortably with that result. Karl Popper, most famously, argued that science does not in fact proceed by induction at all. Scientists propose bold conjectures and then try to refute them; a theory that survives severe testing is not thereby made probable, merely not yet falsified. Critics reply that this evasion only relocates the problem. If we rely on well-tested theories to build bridges and prescribe drugs, we are betting that they will keep working, and that bet looks like an inductive one.

The second camp seeks a justification that does not beg the question. Some argue that induction is simply part of what we mean by rational inference, so that asking whether induction is reasonable is like asking whether the law is legal. Others, following Hans Reichenbach, offer a pragmatic vindication: if nature has any regularities at all, then induction will eventually find them, whereas no other method can do better, and if nature has none, no method will succeed. Induction is thus the best bet available even if we cannot show it is a good bet. The weakness of this argument is that it guarantees only convergence in the long run, which says little about the reliability of any particular prediction we must make today.

Nelson Goodman sharpened the puzzle in a different direction. Define "grue" as the property of being green if examined before some future date and blue otherwise. Every emerald examined so far is both green and grue, so the evidence supports "all emeralds are green" and "all emeralds are grue" equally well, yet the two hypotheses predict different colors for emeralds examined after the date. The lesson Goodman drew is that the trouble lies not only in justifying the step from past to future but in saying which regularities are projectible at all. Our practice favors green over grue, but the favoritism seems to rest on entrenchment, the history of our own predicates, rather than on any feature of the world that logic can detect.

It would be a mistake to conclude that the problem is merely academic. Medicine, engineering, and everyday life all depend on projecting patterns forward, and the skeptic's question forces us to see that this dependence is a commitment rather than a deduction. Perhaps the most honest position is that induction is not something we adopt after weighing reasons but something we cannot do without, and that philosophy's task is to clarify what kind of necessity this is.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Pragmatic and linguistic arguments have refuted Hume's challenge, so confidence in induction is now fully secure.
options.B: Popper's falsificationism shows science needs no assumption about the future, so Hume's problem has become irrelevant.
options.C: Goodman's grue paradox proves that past observations can never support any generalization about unobserved cases.
options.D: Induction resists non-circular justification, and each major philosophical response to that fact leaves a difficulty unresolved.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage presents Hume's problem and then shows that Popper, the ordinary-language view, Reichenbach, and Goodman each face a remaining difficulty. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the responses fall short, so none of them is described as having refuted Hume. B) Critics in the passage argue Popper only relocates the problem, so it does not become irrelevant. C) Goodman's puzzle concerns which regularities are projectible, not whether all generalizations fail.
questions.trap: Choosing an option built from a single vivid example (grue or Popper) instead of the passage-wide thesis.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the weakness of Reichenbach's pragmatic vindication of induction?

options.A: It supposes that nature has no regularities, which would make every predictive method equally likely to fail.
options.B: It guarantees success only in the long run and says little about any single prediction that must be made now.
options.C: It relies on a definition of rational inference that already counts inductive practice as reasonable by fiat.
options.D: It concedes that some competing method could outperform induction whenever nature happens to be uniform.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage states that the argument ensures only long-run convergence, which says little about today's prediction. Why the others are wrong: A) Reichenbach considers both cases, with and without regularities; he does not assume there are none. C) That is the ordinary-language response, not Reichenbach's pragmatic argument. D) Reichenbach claims no other method can do better than induction, the opposite of this option.
questions.trap: Confusing the pragmatic argument with the ordinary-language argument, which both appear in the same paragraph.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of 'grue' is intended mainly to show that:

options.A: emeralds are likely to change color when examined after some date far enough in the future., as the grue hypothesis implies
options.B: past evidence alone does not settle which generalizations are suitable to project into the future.
options.C: Hume was mistaken in claiming that expectation arises from habit produced by repetition.
options.D: green is a logically more basic property than blue and so deserves priority in inference.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Both 'green' and 'grue' fit the evidence equally, so the problem includes selecting projectible regularities. Why the others are wrong: A) The example is a thought experiment about predicates, not a prediction about emeralds. C) Goodman's puzzle extends Hume's skepticism and does not dispute the role of habit. D) The passage says logic detects no feature favoring green; the preference comes from entrenchment.
questions.trap: Reading the thought experiment literally as a claim about emeralds rather than about predicates.

questions.stem: The remark that asking whether induction is reasonable is 'like asking whether the law is legal' suggests that:

options.A: the standard by which induction is being judged is itself partly defined by inductive practice.
options.B: legal reasoning is the best available model for how scientists should evaluate predictions about nature.
options.C: the question of induction's reasonableness is meaningless because no one actually relies on induction.
options.D: the justification of induction can be completed by appeal to a precedent established in past cases.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The analogy implies that the thing under evaluation also supplies the standard of evaluation, as the law supplies legality. Why the others are wrong: B) The analogy concerns circularity of standards, not the adoption of legal methods in science. C) The passage stresses that medicine and everyday life depend on induction. D) Appealing to past cases would itself be an inductive step and is not what the analogy conveys.
questions.trap: Taking the legal analogy as a recommendation about legal reasoning instead of an illustration of standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of the 'commitment rather than a deduction' described in the final paragraph?

options.A: A mathematician proving that the sum of two even numbers must always be even., whatever particular numbers are chosen to begin with
options.B: A logician showing that a conclusion cannot be false if its premises are true., whatever the subject matter of the argument
options.C: A geometer deriving the angle sum of a triangle from a set of stated axioms.
options.D: A physician prescribing a drug on the basis that it has worked in earlier patients with the same condition.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Prescribing on the basis of past outcomes projects a pattern forward without deductive warrant. Why the others are wrong: A) A proof is a deduction, so no projection from past cases is involved. B) Validity of a deduction is guaranteed by the premises, with no commitment about the future. C) Deriving results from axioms is deductive reasoning, not a bet on continued regularity.
questions.trap: Picking an example of certainty because it sounds rigorous, when the passage links commitment to projecting patterns.

questions.stem: The author's concluding stance toward induction is best described as:

options.A: optimistic expectation that philosophers will eventually derive induction from purely logical premises.
options.B: candid acceptance that it is unavoidable, with a call to clarify its kind of necessity.
options.C: dismissive suggestion that the skeptic's challenge matters only to academics and not to real practice.
options.D: firm endorsement of Popper's proposal that science should abandon inductive reasoning altogether.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The last sentence says induction is something we cannot do without and that philosophy should clarify its necessity. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage gives no hope of a logical derivation; Hume showed demonstration is unavailable. C) The author states it would be a mistake to treat the problem as merely academic. D) The author reports Popper's view and a criticism of it, and does not endorse it.
questions.trap: Overlooking that the author explicitly rejects the idea the problem is merely academic.

passages.passage_text:
The two-day weekend feels like a natural feature of the calendar, but it is barely a century old in most of the world, and its history is stranger than its familiarity suggests. A weekly rest day is ancient: the seven-day cycle, with its day of cessation from labor, passed from Jewish practice into Christian and later Islamic observance, each tradition fixing a different day as sacred. What medieval Europe lacked was not rest but regularity. Saints' days and festivals interrupted work irregularly, and by some estimates the common laborer enjoyed more days off than his nineteenth-century descendant, though at times set by the church and the agricultural season rather than by the clock.

The factory disrupted this older rhythm. Industrial employers wanted predictable hours and a labor force that appeared reliably at the machines. Yet workers resisted, and one of their most durable customs was "Saint Monday," the practice of extending Sunday's leisure into the first day of the week, especially among skilled artisans paid by the piece. Employers complained of absenteeism and hangovers; workers regarded the day as a right. The compromise that eventually emerged in English textile towns was the half-holiday on Saturday afternoon, which traded a portion of Monday's freedom for an earlier, legally protected release at the end of the week. The "Saturday half" later acquired a life of its own, as football matches, music halls, and excursion trains grew up to fill it.

The full two-day weekend arrived piecemeal. In the United States, a New England cotton mill reportedly accommodated Jewish workers by closing on both Saturday and Sunday early in the twentieth century, but the decisive shift came in the 1920s and 1930s. Henry Ford's decision in 1926 to adopt a five-day, forty-hour week in his plants is often cited as a turning point. Ford's motives were mixed. He acknowledged that shorter hours might raise productivity, but he also argued that workers with leisure would become consumers of the goods they made, including automobiles. The Depression gave the idea further force, since shortening the week appeared to spread scarce jobs among more workers, and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 made forty hours the national standard for overtime pay.

It would be tempting to tell this story as one of benevolent progress, but historians caution against that. The weekend was won through decades of organized pressure from unions, and its benefits were unevenly shared: domestic servants, farm workers, and many service employees were excluded from the legislation that protected factory hands. Nor did the weekend simply give people free time. It created a new category of time, leisure, that markets and institutions promptly set about organizing, from the department store sale to the spectator sport.

The recent erosion of the weekend is therefore less a departure than a continuation. As work migrates to screens that are always at hand, and as retail and healthcare operate around the clock, the boundary between work and rest is again becoming negotiable. What the history of the weekend suggests is that such boundaries are never given by nature. They are institutions, built by particular conflicts among employers, workers, and governments, and they last only as long as people are willing to defend them.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that the modern weekend:

options.A: arose naturally from ancient religious cycles of rest and has changed very little in its basic form since.
options.B: was produced by specific economic interests and labor struggles, and so is an institution that must be defended.
options.C: was granted by employers who recognized that fatigue lowers output and who acted entirely out of benevolence., with no pressure from workers
options.D: has been permanently secured by legislation and so is no longer threatened by changes in the nature of work.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage traces the weekend through conflicts among workers, employers, and governments and ends by calling such boundaries institutions. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the weekend is barely a century old and its history is stranger than it seems. C) The author cautions against telling the story as benevolent progress. D) The final paragraph describes the weekend as currently eroding, so it is not permanently secure.
questions.trap: Accepting the familiar 'natural calendar' story that the opening sentence is set up to challenge.

questions.stem: According to the passage, 'Saint Monday' was:

options.A: a church festival that required factories to close on the first day of each week throughout the year.
options.B: an employer program that rewarded punctual workers with a paid day of leisure at the start of the week.
options.C: a legal holiday established for artisans after unions secured the forty-hour week in the United States.
options.D: a worker custom of prolonging Sunday leisure, which employers resisted and which gave way to the Saturday half-holiday.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage describes it as a customary extension of Sunday that employers called absenteeism and that led to the compromise of the half-holiday. Why the others are wrong: A) It was a worker custom, not an ecclesiastical requirement. B) Employers complained about it, so it was not an employer reward. C) It was a nineteenth-century custom, which predates the legislation of 1938.
questions.trap: Assuming a named day must be an official holiday rather than an informal worker practice.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Henry Ford's adoption of the five-day week in 1926 was motivated by:

options.A: a conviction that workers deserve rest regardless of any effect on the company's output or sales.
options.B: a legal obligation created by earlier legislation that mandated forty hours as the standard work week., which employers followed reluctantly
options.C: a desire to spread scarce jobs among more workers during the economic collapse of the 1930s.
options.D: a combination of expected productivity gains and the hope that leisured workers would buy the products they made.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The text says his motives were mixed: productivity and cultivating consumers. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage calls his motives mixed, and both aims were commercial. B) The Fair Labor Standards Act came in 1938, after Ford's decision. C) The job-sharing rationale is attached to the Depression, which began after 1926.
questions.trap: Ignoring the chronology: the Depression and the 1938 law came after Ford's move.

questions.stem: The passage implies that, compared with a nineteenth-century factory worker, a medieval European laborer:

options.A: may have had more days free from work, though those days were fixed by religious and seasonal rhythms.
options.B: worked fewer hours per day because tasks were easily completed by hand and with little supervision., unlike workers in factories
options.C: enjoyed a regular weekly schedule that was set by the clock and enforced by employers.
options.D: had no concept of a weekly day of rest because the seven-day cycle was introduced later.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says medieval workers had more days off by some estimates, set by the church and agriculture, not by the clock. Why the others are wrong: B) Hours per day are not discussed; the comparison concerns days off. C) The passage says medieval Europe lacked regularity; clock-based schedules belong to the factory. D) The seven-day cycle is described as ancient, passing from Jewish practice into later traditions.
questions.trap: Treating 'regular' and 'frequent' as the same thing when the passage separates them.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the benefits of the weekend were unevenly shared?

options.A: Records from the 1940s show that factory employees took more days of leave than they had before the war.
options.B: Records from the 1940s show that department stores earned more on Saturdays than on any other day of the week.
options.C: Records from the 1940s show that farm laborers and household servants worked more hours per week than factory employees.
options.D: Records from the 1940s show that many unions bargained successfully for shorter working hours in factories.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Longer hours for excluded workers directly supports the claim that protections favored factory hands over others. Why the others are wrong: A) This concerns factory workers only and says nothing about those left out. B) Store revenue speaks to leisure markets, not to who got the weekend. D) Union success in factories is consistent with, but does not show, exclusion of other workers.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that is about the weekend generally and not about who was excluded from it.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the author's claim that recent erosion of the weekend is 'a continuation' implies that:

options.A: the weekend's decline reflects a failure of workers to appreciate the history they have inherited.
options.B: digital technology is the first force in history to threaten established limits on working hours.
options.C: the boundary between work and rest has always depended on conflict and can be renegotiated.
options.D: governments should abandon laws that regulate hours because markets will determine suitable limits.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) If boundaries are institutions built by conflict, their present loosening is another episode of the same process. Why the others are wrong: A) The author blames no failure of appreciation; boundaries last as long as people defend them. B) Calling it a continuation means it is not the first such force. D) The passage makes no case against regulation.
questions.trap: Reading a historical observation as a policy recommendation the author never makes.

passages.passage_text:
The sonnet is among the most confining of poetic forms, and yet it has been renewed by poets for more than seven centuries. Fourteen lines, a fixed rhyme scheme, and a metrical norm of five stresses per line leave little room for improvisation. Critics have often treated this as a puzzle: why would a writer choose to work in a form whose rules are so exacting, when the modern tradition prizes freedom? One answer, favored by those who see form as a kind of resistance, is that constraint is productive. A poet who must find a rhyme for "love" cannot say whatever first comes to mind, and the search for an acceptable word may uncover a thought that unconstrained writing would never have reached.

The two principal varieties of the form divide their material differently. The Petrarchan sonnet pairs an octave, rhyming abbaabba, with a sestet whose pattern varies, and this division encourages a movement from problem to response, or from observation to reflection. The Shakespearean sonnet, three quatrains and a closing couplet, favors a different structure: it allows the poet to develop an idea in three variations and then to turn, often with epigrammatic force, in the final two lines. In both kinds the volta, or turn, is the crucial event. A sonnet is rarely a single thought held steady for fourteen lines; it is a thought that meets resistance and changes direction.

Skeptics point out that the English language is poorly suited to the form. Italian, with its many words ending in vowels, supplies rhymes in abundance, whereas English is comparatively poor in them, and the Petrarchan scheme's demand for four rhymes on a single sound can force awkward syntax. Yet this difficulty may be less a defect than a source of the form's distinctive character in English. Poets of the Romantic period, among them Wordsworth, spoke of the sonnet as a small space in which they could be "bound" and thereby find unexpected freedom, and later poets stretched the rules rather than abandoning them, using slant rhyme, irregular meter, or subjects unimaginable to Petrarch.

The modern sonnet shows how far that stretching can go. Some twentieth-century poets wrote sonnets on political violence, racial injustice, or the discomforts of domestic life, retaining the fourteen lines while loosening nearly everything else. The effect is often one of tension between the received form and a content that seems to strain against it, a tension that readers familiar with the tradition feel as a kind of argument. A poem in which an ordinary kitchen quarrel is compressed into a Petrarchan octave makes a claim, however faintly, about the dignity of ordinary experience.

Whether the constraints of the sonnet liberate or merely limit is perhaps the wrong question. The form's persistence suggests that writers value it not because its rules are justified in the abstract but because they provide a shared set of expectations against which individual choices become visible. A departure from the rhyme scheme means something only when the scheme is known. In this sense the sonnet's rules function less as a cage than as a language, one that gives each deliberate violation its meaning.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of the sonnet's constraints?

options.A: They are artificial burdens that modern poets would be wise to discard in favor of free verse.
options.B: They are justified in the abstract because they guarantee superior poetry to unrestricted writing.
options.C: They suit Italian poets but doom English poets to awkward, unnatural syntax in nearly every poem.
options.D: They matter less as limits than as shared expectations that make departures meaningful.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The final paragraph says the rules function as a language that gives each violation its meaning. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the persistence of the form suggests writers value it, so it should not be discarded. B) The author says the rules are not justified in the abstract, so no guarantee of quality is claimed. C) The author treats the English difficulty as possibly a source of character, not as doom.
questions.trap: Choosing the answer that matches the opening puzzle rather than the author's resolution at the end.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the volta is:

options.A: a change of direction in the poem's thought, which is the crucial event in both major kinds of sonnet.
options.B: a rhyming couplet that appears only at the close of the Shakespearean form and never in other types. of poem
options.C: an octave of eight lines whose rhyme scheme must be repeated exactly in the sestet that follows it.
options.D: a metrical device that lets poets vary the number of stresses in a line when the rhyme requires it.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage calls the turn the crucial event in both varieties, where a thought meets resistance and changes direction. Why the others are wrong: B) The couplet is a structural part of the Shakespearean form, but the volta is the turn, not the couplet itself. C) The passage says the sestet's pattern varies and does not repeat the octave's. D) The volta concerns the movement of thought, not meter.
questions.trap: Equating the turn with the closing couplet because the couplet often carries it in the Shakespearean form.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that English is poorly suited to the sonnet is best described as:

options.A: agreeing wholeheartedly that the scarcity of rhymes has permanently limited what English sonnets can achieve.
options.B: rejecting the claim by showing that English contains as many rhyming words as Italian does.
options.C: acknowledging the difficulty while suggesting it may help produce the form's distinctive English character.
options.D: ignoring the claim as irrelevant to the larger question of why poets choose the sonnet form.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author grants the scarcity of rhymes but says the difficulty may be a source of distinctive character. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not agree that the limit is permanent; later poets stretched the rules. B) The author concedes English is poorer in rhymes and offers no contrary data. D) The author addresses the claim directly in a full paragraph.
questions.trap: Treating a concession as total agreement and missing the author's 'yet' pivot.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a modern sonnet compressing a domestic quarrel into a Petrarchan octave would:

options.A: fail as a sonnet because the Petrarchan octave is suited only to the great themes of love and religion.
options.B: demonstrate that the form has been fully emptied of meaning and now serves merely as decoration.
options.C: show that content is unimportant to a sonnet provided its rhyme and meter follow the conventions.
options.D: create tension between form and content that implicitly claims dignity for everyday life.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says such poems make a claim about the dignity of ordinary experience through tension between form and content. Why the others are wrong: A) No limit on themes is stated; the passage says modern poets used many subjects. B) The passage treats the tension as meaningful, not as decoration. C) The example shows content and form interacting, which makes content important.
questions.trap: Assuming that unusual content must be a sign the form is failing or exhausted.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that constraint is productive in sonnet writing?

options.A: Drafts show that sonneteers usually compose a complete thought in prose and then fit it to the rhyme scheme without altering the content.
options.B: Drafts show that sonneteers often replace a first-choice word with a rhyme that they judge to be more surprising.
options.C: Drafts show that sonneteers sometimes spend days searching for a rhyme and then revise the neighboring lines.
options.D: Drafts show that sonneteers who write many sonnets in a row tend to explore a widening range of subjects.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) If rhyme requirements never alter the content, then constraint is not generating new thoughts, which weakens the claim. Why the others are wrong: B) Replacing words for a surprising rhyme supports the claim. C) Searching and revising neighboring lines suggests the constraint shapes content, which supports the claim. D) Widening subjects across sonnets is neutral or favorable to the claim.
questions.trap: Selecting a detail about effort rather than one that bears on whether constraint changes content.

questions.stem: The comparison of the sonnet's rules to a language in the last paragraph serves mainly to:

options.A: suggest that the sonnet should be taught in schools as a model of correct grammar and composition.
options.B: argue that sonnet rules, like those of grammar, have changed little across more than seven centuries.
options.C: illustrate that deliberate rule-breaking is meaningful only against a background of rules both poet and reader know.
options.D: show that most readers experience the sonnet as a cage until they have mastered its vocabulary.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A language gives meaning to violations, as the next sentence says: a departure means something only when the scheme is known. Why the others are wrong: A) The analogy is about meaning, not education. B) The passage shows the rules have been stretched across the centuries. D) The passage says the rules function less as a cage.
questions.trap: Importing a claim about teaching or history that the analogy does not make.

passages.passage_text:
Few forms of art provoke as dependable a quarrel over legitimacy as street art. A mural painted without permission on the side of a warehouse is, in the eyes of the law, a trespass or an act of property damage; in the eyes of a gallery owner, it may be a commodity worth six figures once the wall is cut out and sold. The same object can be a crime and a masterpiece, and the question of which it is seems to depend less on anything about the image than on who is entitled to decide. For this reason, debates about street art tend to be debates about authority: who may speak in public space, who is licensed to confer the status of art, and what is lost when that license is granted.

The earliest graffiti writers of the late twentieth century understood their work as an assertion of presence by people who were otherwise invisible in the city. Tags, repeated until the name itself became a kind of insignia, claimed turf and reputation, and the risk of arrest was part of the point. The ordinary citizen, seeing only vandalism, mistook an elaborate code of skill and peer recognition for chaos. That code had its own standards of legitimacy, in which style, location, and daring were judged by other writers rather than by critics or officials.

When museums and collectors began to acquire such work, a new form of legitimacy arrived, and with it a dilemma. Institutional recognition brought money, preservation, and public attention to artists who had long gone unrewarded. But it also detached the work from the conditions that gave it meaning. An image painted on a canvas to be hung in a collector's living room has lost the illegality, the impermanence, and the confrontation with passersby that defined it in the street. Some artists have embraced the market; others have deliberately courted destruction, as when a painting is made to shred itself moments after it is sold, mocking the very act of valuation.

A second form of legitimacy comes from municipalities that commission murals or designate "legal walls." Here the work is permitted, and often it is celebrated as a tool of neighborhood renewal. Yet critics argue that commissioned street art can serve as a decorative gloss on gentrification, brightening districts shortly before rents rise and long-time residents are displaced. In this view, the legal mural is not the triumph of street art but its domestication, an official use of an outsider's idiom to signal a vibrancy that policy has not otherwise provided.

It would be too simple to conclude either that sanctioned street art is inauthentic or that illegal work is automatically authentic. Authenticity is not a property that a wall carries with it; it is a judgment made by audiences, and audiences differ. The more interesting lesson may be that the legitimacy of any art form is never secured once and for all. Each new institution that embraces street art changes what the practice means, and each change prompts some practitioners to seek the margins again, where legitimacy has yet to be bestowed.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole is chiefly concerned with:

options.A: why street artists should be prosecuted when they paint on private property without the owner's consent.
options.B: which techniques distinguish valuable murals from ordinary graffiti in the judgment of professional critics.
options.C: how gentrification has destroyed the communities that originally produced street art in major cities.
options.D: how recognition from different authorities confers legitimacy on street art while altering what the work means.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage walks through the legal, museum, and municipal forms of legitimacy and notes that each changes the practice. Why the others are wrong: A) The author takes no side on prosecution; the point is about authority. B) The passage says early graffiti judged itself by peers, not critics, and does not rank techniques. C) Gentrification is raised only as a criticism of commissioned murals.
questions.trap: Latching onto the gentrification criticism, which is only one part of the argument.

questions.stem: The author mentions a painting made to shred itself after being sold in order to:

options.A: show that illegal street work is inevitably destroyed by the authorities soon after it is painted.
options.B: demonstrate that museums prefer works that cannot be preserved or exhibited for long periods.
options.C: argue that artists who join the art market always abandon the principles of their earlier work.
options.D: illustrate an artist's attempt to mock the act by which the market assigns value to art.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says some artists court destruction, mocking the very act of valuation. Why the others are wrong: A) The shredding occurs after a sale and is the artist's choice, not the authorities' action. B) The passage says nothing about museum preferences for impermanence. C) The passage says some embrace the market and others resist; it does not say all abandon principles.
questions.trap: Reading an illustration of resistance as a general claim about the market's effect on all artists.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the earliest graffiti writers differed from ordinary citizens in that they:

options.A: regarded their tags as vandalism but defended them as a necessary protest against private property.
options.B: sought approval from critics and officials who could grant their work a place in the art world. as quickly as they could
options.C: judged work by an internal code in which style, location, and daring earned recognition from other writers.
options.D: avoided repeated names in order to prevent police from identifying them across the city.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage says peers, not critics or officials, judged style, location, and daring. Why the others are wrong: A) The writers saw tags as claims of presence, not as vandalism. B) The passage says standards came from other writers rather than critics or officials. D) The passage says names were repeated until they became insignia.
questions.trap: Assuming the writers shared the outsiders' view that their work was disorder.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the critics' claim that commissioned murals can serve as a gloss on gentrification?

options.A: Visitors to districts with city-installed murals reported greater enjoyment than those in other districts.
options.B: Rents rose faster in districts where the city installed murals than in similar districts where it did not.
options.C: Muralists commissioned by the city reported that their work was less controversial than unsanctioned pieces.
options.D: Districts with legal walls showed a larger number of new galleries than districts without such walls.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Faster rent increases tied to mural installation directly support the claim of a link to displacement. Why the others are wrong: A) Enjoyment says nothing about displacement or rents. C) Reduced controversy concerns reception of the art, not housing. D) More galleries may relate to culture, but it does not demonstrate rising rents or displacement.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about popularity or cultural activity instead of the economic harm the critics assert.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is most consistent with the author's view of authenticity in the final paragraph?

options.A: A commissioned mural may seem authentic to one group of viewers and contrived to another group.
options.B: A mural is authentic only if it has been painted without the permission of the property's owner.
options.C: A mural becomes authentic once a museum acquires it and certifies its place in the canon.
options.D: A mural is authentic whenever the artist's intentions are sincere, regardless of any audience's view.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says authenticity is a judgment made by audiences, who differ. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says illegal work is not automatically authentic. C) The author says no institution secures legitimacy once and for all. D) The author locates authenticity in audience judgment, not in the artist's sincerity alone.
questions.trap: Equating illegality with authenticity, a view the author calls too simple.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of the dilemma described in the third paragraph?

options.A: A city sells a permit to a writer, who then paints a larger mural than the permit allows on a public wall.
options.B: A writer earns a living when a gallery buys a mural, but the transferred work loses its confrontation with passersby.
options.C: A collector commissions a mural for a private lobby and the artist is paid but the work is never publicly seen.
options.D: A writer paints over an earlier mural and is arrested for the damage to the property of another artist.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Recognition brings money and attention but removes the conditions that gave the work meaning. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a permit violation, not a trade-off between recognition and meaning. C) The work is made for a collector, with no loss of street context it had previously. D) This concerns property damage between artists and not institutional recognition.
questions.trap: Choosing an example with art and money but without the loss of original context.

passages.passage_text:
In 1952 the composer John Cage sat in a hall in Woodstock, New York, while pianist David Tudor sat at the piano for four minutes and thirty-three seconds without playing a note. The audience, expecting music, heard instead the rustle of the wind in the trees, the patter of rain on the roof, and the murmurs of their own discomfort. Cage later said that the piece taught him there is no such thing as silence, only sounds one has not chosen to listen to. The work remains the most notorious statement in the long and underappreciated history of silence in music, a history that begins well before Cage and extends well beyond the gestures he made famous.

Even in conventional notation, silence is a structural element, not an absence. The rest is written as carefully as the note, and composers have long exploited its power. Mozart's pauses create suspense by delaying an expected resolution, and Beethoven's famous interruptions, in which a sustained passage halts abruptly, make the listener aware of the continuity that has just been broken. The hush before an orchestral climax does the opposite of what we might suppose: it does not diminish the loud passage but intensifies it, because contrast is how the ear measures magnitude. A fortissimo preceded by a bar of nothing sounds louder than the same chord arriving after a crescendo.

Silence also shapes the way listeners attend. In a concert hall the audience's own quiet is a precondition for hearing the softest passages, and the custom of withholding applause between movements, now loosening, was an attempt to preserve a long arc of tension that clapping would dissipate. By contrast, many non-Western traditions treat silence as a form of participation. In Japanese aesthetics the notion of ma, the interval between events, is regarded not as empty space but as the medium that gives events their shape. A pause in a performance of gagaku or in a noh play is part of the substance of the work.

The modern world complicates all of this. Recorded music flows through earbuds and shops and elevators, so that silence has become scarce, and it is therefore tempting to see the intentional quiet of a composer as a form of protest against the saturated acoustic environment. Some listeners do hear it this way. Yet there is a risk of overreading. A rest in a Haydn quartet is hardly a critique of consumer culture; it is part of a rhetoric of surprise that the composer's audience understood. Reading present anxieties into the past can obscure the particular work that silence did in each period.

What unites these uses of silence is the recognition that music is not simply sound but sound organized in time, and that time includes intervals in which nothing is played. Cage's provocation was less a rejection of music than an extension of its logic. By removing every note, he asked the audience to hear what the frame of a concert had always done: it makes us listen. That an act of attention can be the substance of a musical work is a thought that earlier composers had implied, but Cage insisted upon it so uncomfortably that it could no longer be ignored.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with showing that silence in music:

options.A: is best understood as a modern form of protest against the noise of contemporary consumer culture.
options.B: was an invention of John Cage that had no precedent in earlier traditions of Western composition.
options.C: serves structural, attentional, and cultural functions, which Cage's piece pushed to an extreme.
options.D: is a purely visual feature of written scores that listeners generally do not perceive in performance.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage moves from Cage to rests in Mozart and Beethoven, audience quiet, ma, and then Cage again. Why the others are wrong: A) The author warns against reading silence as protest against consumer culture. B) The author says silence had a history well before Cage. D) The author says rests are heard and shape expectation.
questions.trap: Following the author's tempting modern-protest reading that the fourth paragraph actually cautions against.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Cage's piece demonstrated that:

options.A: a pianist can create tension by refusing to play when an audience expects a performance to begin.
options.B: sounds in the environment become part of a musical experience when an audience attends to them.
options.C: audiences find music more meaningful when it is performed in total acoustic isolation from the world.
options.D: a complete absence of sound is possible only in a concert hall designed to exclude outside noise.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Cage said there is no silence, only sounds one has not chosen to listen to; wind, rain, and murmurs were heard. Why the others are wrong: A) The point was not tension from refusal but the sounds that were present. C) The audience heard environmental sounds, so isolation was not achieved or sought. D) Cage's remark implies silence is never fully attainable anywhere.
questions.trap: Treating the work as a stunt about the performer's refusal rather than a lesson about listening.

questions.stem: The passage explains that a fortissimo chord following a bar of rest sounds louder than the same chord after a crescendo because:

options.A: the ear judges loudness by contrast with what has come immediately before.
options.B: the silence allows the orchestra to play with greater force than is possible after sustained playing.
options.C: listeners are more attentive after a pause and therefore perceive a higher actual volume of sound.
options.D: composers always write louder dynamic markings for chords that come after a rest.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says contrast is how the ear measures magnitude. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage explains an effect in perception, not in how hard the players play. C) Attention is not the stated cause; contrast is. D) The passage does not discuss dynamic markings.
questions.trap: Substituting a plausible physical explanation for the perceptual one the author gives.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the contrast the passage draws between concert-hall quiet and the Japanese concept of ma?

options.A: Concert quiet is a Western custom that is now vanishing, whereas ma is a recent aesthetic adopted by Western composers.
options.B: Concert quiet shows respect for the performers, whereas ma is a means of silencing the audience during rituals.
options.C: Concert quiet is a feature of notation, whereas ma is a matter of the audience's behavior in the hall.
options.D: Concert quiet is a condition for hearing the music, whereas ma treats the interval itself as part of the work.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says audience quiet allows soft passages to be heard, while ma is the medium that gives events their shape. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage calls ma a long-standing notion in Japanese aesthetics and not a recent Western adoption. B) The passage does not describe ma as silencing an audience. C) This reverses the two: rests are notated, and concert quiet concerns the audience.
questions.trap: Reversing which type of silence belongs to the audience and which to the work.

questions.stem: The author's caution in the fourth paragraph about 'overreading' would apply most directly to which of the following claims?

options.A: That a rest in a Haydn quartet was intended as a criticism of the streaming services of our era.
options.B: That a rest in a Haydn quartet builds suspense by delaying a resolution the listener expects.
options.C: That a rest in a Haydn quartet is notated with the same care as the notes surrounding it.
options.D: That a rest in a Haydn quartet contributes to a rhetoric of surprise that audiences of his time understood.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author warns against reading present anxieties into past works, which this anachronistic claim does. Why the others are wrong: B) Suspense through delay is the kind of historical function the author endorses. C) Careful notation of rests is stated in the passage. D) The author says Haydn's rest is part of a rhetoric of surprise his audience understood.
questions.trap: Missing that the other options match the author's own historically grounded claims.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, in relation to earlier composers, Cage:

options.A: stated openly and insistently an idea about attention that their work had only implied.
options.B: abandoned the fundamental assumption that music is sound organized in time.
options.C: rejected the structural use of rests that composers such as Mozart had explored.
options.D: introduced the notion that listening is an activity that concert audiences must be taught.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The last sentence says earlier composers implied that an act of attention could be the substance of a work and Cage insisted on it. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says Cage extended music's logic and did not abandon it. C) Cage built on the importance of silence; he did not reject it. D) The passage says the concert frame always made us listen, so the notion was not new.
questions.trap: Overstating Cage's break with tradition, which the author deliberately qualifies.

passages.passage_text:
Trust is among the most pervasive and least visible foundations of social life. We eat food prepared by strangers, deposit money in institutions whose vaults we will never see, and take medicines on the word of professionals whose training we cannot evaluate. If each of these acts required independent verification, ordinary life would grind to a halt. Sociologists have therefore long regarded trust as a mechanism for coping with complexity: it allows us to act as though uncertain things were settled, and so to cooperate with people whose intentions and competence we cannot fully know.

A common distinction separates particularized trust, which attaches to specific people with whom we have a history, from generalized trust, which extends to strangers and to institutions. The first is easy to understand. We trust a neighbor because we have watched her behave reliably, and we know that she cares about her reputation among people we both know. The second is harder to explain, because strangers cannot be monitored and offer no prospect of repeated dealings. Some scholars argue that generalized trust is produced by dense networks of voluntary association, from choirs to bowling leagues, in which people learn habits of reciprocity that spread outward. Others contend that it depends less on civic habits than on the reliability of formal institutions, such as courts that enforce contracts and police who are not corrupt. On this second view, people are willing to trust strangers because they believe that betrayal will be punished.

The relationship between the two accounts is an active area of debate. Cross-national surveys have found that societies with higher levels of generalized trust tend also to have lower corruption and stronger economies, but the direction of causation is difficult to establish. Trust may promote prosperity by lowering the cost of transactions, or prosperity may encourage trust by reducing the threat that strangers pose to one's livelihood. Both processes may operate together, forming a cycle that can be virtuous or vicious. Where institutions fail, people retreat to family and clan, whose members they can monitor, and this retreat weakens the institutions further.

Trust is also unevenly distributed within societies. Individuals who have been the victims of discrimination or of institutional neglect may rationally distrust the very bodies that others take for granted, and their distrust is not a character flaw but a reasonable inference from experience. Public-health campaigns that fail to recognize this often attribute low participation to ignorance, when its source is a history of broken promises. Rebuilding trust under these conditions requires evidence of changed behavior sustained over time, and cannot be accomplished by appeals alone.

The fragility of trust is also its peculiar feature. It accumulates slowly, through many small acts of reliability, and can be destroyed in an instant by a single betrayal that appears to reveal a hidden truth about the trusted party. This asymmetry explains why institutions guard their reputations so anxiously, and why scandals that seem trivial in scale may produce long-lasting damage. Trust, in this sense, is less a possession than a relationship that must be continuously renewed.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: argue that trust in strangers should be replaced by systematic verification wherever possible.
options.B: describe how trust enables cooperation among strangers and examine debates over where it comes from.
options.C: prove that societies with greater wealth always have citizens who trust one another more.
options.D: show that distrust among marginalized groups results mainly from ignorance of how institutions work.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage defines trust as a way of coping with complexity and then compares explanations of generalized trust. Why the others are wrong: A) The opening paragraph says verification of everything is impossible. C) The author says causation between trust and prosperity is unclear. D) The author says that distrust is a reasonable inference from experience, not ignorance.
questions.trap: Taking a single supporting claim as the purpose of the entire passage.

questions.stem: A person who lends power tools to a neighbor of twenty years, expecting their return, is best described as showing:

options.A: particularized trust grounded in a history of the neighbor's reliable behavior and concern for reputation.
options.B: generalized trust grounded in confidence that courts would enforce any agreement between neighbors.
options.C: generalized trust produced by membership in voluntary associations such as choirs or bowling leagues.
options.D: institutional trust arising from a belief that betrayal of a neighbor will be punished by police.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage ties particularized trust to people we know and have watched behave reliably. Why the others are wrong: B) The relationship rests on personal history, not courts. C) The example does not involve voluntary associations or strangers. D) The example concerns a known person, not an institution.
questions.trap: Confusing the scale of the relationship; the trust here attaches to a known individual.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most support the view that generalized trust depends on reliable institutions?

options.A: Residents of a town with many choirs and clubs report high trust in neighbors but little trust in courts.
options.B: Citizens of a country with corrupt courts show higher trust in strangers after joining local associations.
options.C: Immigrants who move to a country with honest courts show rising trust in strangers even if they join no voluntary groups.
options.D: Members of tightly knit clans report that they trust their relatives more than they trust strangers.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Trust rising after exposure to honest institutions, without civic groups, favors the institutional account. Why the others are wrong: A) This pattern favors the civic-association account or at least the independence of trust from institutions. B) This suggests associations matter even where institutions are poor, which supports the civic account. D) Trust in relatives is particularized trust and does not bear on the source of generalized trust.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that supports the rival associational account.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of the link between national trust levels and prosperity indicates that the correlation:

options.A: demonstrates that trust causes prosperity by lowering the transaction costs in an economy.
options.B: demonstrates that prosperity causes trust by lessening the threat strangers pose to livelihood. in the world's poorest nations
options.C: is an artifact of survey methods and disappears when corruption is held constant statistically.
options.D: does not by itself reveal its causal direction, since trust and prosperity might each strengthen the other.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says the direction is difficult to establish and that both processes may operate in a cycle. Why the others are wrong: A) This is one hypothesis the author presents, but not as proven. B) This is the other hypothesis and also not proven. C) The passage says nothing of an artifact of surveys.
questions.trap: Selecting one of two hypotheses that the author deliberately leaves open.

questions.stem: The author would most likely interpret low participation in a health campaign among a community with a history of institutional neglect as:

options.A: a sign that members of the community lack the education needed to evaluate health information.
options.B: a reasonable response to experience that calls for sustained evidence of change.
options.C: an irrational reaction that disappears once the campaign provides appeals and clearer messages.
options.D: a consequence of particularized trust, which always blocks acceptance of new institutions.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says such distrust is a reasonable inference and that rebuilding requires sustained changed behavior, not appeals alone. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says campaigns wrongly blame ignorance. C) The passage says appeals alone cannot rebuild trust, and the distrust is not irrational. D) Nothing in the passage says particularized trust always blocks new institutions.
questions.trap: Falling back on the ignorance explanation the passage specifically criticizes.

questions.stem: According to the final paragraph, institutions guard their reputations anxiously because:

options.A: scandals that are small in scale rarely damage an institution and so are not seriously feared.
options.B: trust accumulates slowly but one apparent betrayal can destroy it by seeming to reveal a hidden truth.
options.C: trust is a possession that, once established, cannot be lost without the consent of those who gave it.
options.D: reputations are easier to build through a single dramatic act than through long-term reliability.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage describes the asymmetry between slow accumulation and sudden destruction. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says trivial scandals can cause lasting damage. C) The author says trust is a relationship that must be renewed, not a possession. D) The passage says reliability must be shown through many small acts.
questions.trap: Reversing the asymmetry between building and losing trust.

passages.passage_text:
In the early twentieth century a map of Europe could be read as a list of the claims of nations, yet the nation as a political ideal is a much younger invention than the maps suggest. Historians of nationalism have long asked why it spread so quickly after the late eighteenth century, and one influential answer, developed by Benedict Anderson, points to the printing press and the market for print. A nation, Anderson argued, is an "imagined community": its members will never meet most of their fellow citizens, yet they carry in their minds the image of their communion. What enabled millions of strangers to imagine themselves as a single people was the experience of reading the same words, in the same language, at roughly the same time.

The mechanism he proposed was concrete. Early printers, seeking markets large enough to repay the cost of their presses, discovered that publishing in Latin reached only a small learned elite, while publishing in the vernacular opened a far greater audience. Over time, the dialects spoken in a region were consolidated into standard languages with fixed spelling and grammar, and these standardized tongues became the property of a literate public. The newspaper then supplied a daily ritual. A person reading the morning paper knew that thousands of others were reading the very same items, and this silent simultaneity gave the nation a kind of reality that no assembly could. Novels, which typically depict characters moving through a shared social space, reinforced the sense that the country was a single stage on which many lives unfolded.

Critics have qualified this account in several ways. Some note that literacy rates in many nineteenth-century states remained low, so that nationalism could not have spread primarily by reading; it was often transmitted by teachers, soldiers, and priests, and by oral performances of songs and stories. Others observe that print could also fragment communities, since publishing in a local vernacular might encourage regional identities that competed with the national one. A third objection concerns the pre-existing materials that nationalists used. Anthony Smith, for example, argued that modern nations typically draw on older ethnic cores, with their myths and memories, and that print did not create these so much as redistribute them.

Anderson's defenders reply that his argument concerns the conditions of possibility for nationalism and not its entire causal history. Print did not manufacture national feeling from nothing, but it made available a new way of imagining belonging, one in which a community could be extended across a territory without face-to-face contact. The relevant comparison is not between literate and illiterate individuals but between societies that had the means of simultaneous communication and societies that did not.

The debate has renewed relevance in an era of digital media. If print enabled the nation, then electronic networks that connect people across borders, and fragment audiences within them, may be reshaping the imagined communities of the present. Whether they will produce larger or smaller forms of belonging is uncertain, but the lesson of the earlier history is that the medium of communication is never neutral with respect to the communities it makes thinkable.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central question of the passage?

options.A: How did the market for print help ordinary people picture themselves as members of national communities?
options.B: Why did nineteenth-century governments choose to require compulsory education in a standard language? for all children
options.C: Which European nation was the first to develop a printing industry that served a popular readership?
options.D: How did Latin lose its place as the language of the educated across the continent of Europe?

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage opens with Anderson's account of print and the imagined community and then examines its criticisms. Why the others are wrong: B) Schooling is mentioned only as a critic's alternative channel. C) The passage names no first nation of print. D) Latin's decline is a detail in the mechanism, not the central question.
questions.trap: Picking a topic touched on in the passage rather than the question that organizes it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the daily newspaper contributed to nationalism chiefly by:

options.A: supplying political parties with a means of recruiting members across regional boundaries.
options.B: assuring each reader that many others were reading the same items at the same moment.
options.C: teaching readers a standardized language that they had not previously encountered in speech.
options.D: depicting characters who move through a shared social space in a continuing series of episodes.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage describes a 'silent simultaneity' that gave the nation reality. Why the others are wrong: A) Recruitment is not discussed. C) Standardization came through print markets generally, not specifically from the newspaper's daily ritual. D) The shared stage of characters is attributed to novels.
questions.trap: Attributing to the newspaper a feature the passage assigns to the novel.

questions.stem: Anthony Smith's position, as described in the passage, is that:

options.A: nationalism arose with the printing press and had no connection to earlier ethnic or religious identities. of any kind
options.B: print tended to divide communities, so national identities could only emerge where literacy was low.
options.C: nations were imagined by teachers, soldiers, and priests who spread nationalism through oral performance.
options.D: modern nations usually build on older ethnic cores, whose myths and memories print redistributed more than created.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says Smith held that print did not create the older materials so much as redistribute them. Why the others are wrong: A) That is closer to Anderson's thesis, which Smith qualifies. B) Fragmentation by vernacular is a separate objection and does not claim national identity needs low literacy. C) The teachers, soldiers, and priests point belongs to the objection about literacy.
questions.trap: Merging separate objections to Anderson into one position.

questions.stem: Which of the following would Anderson's defenders most likely accept as consistent with his argument?

options.A: A population adopts national feeling even though no member has ever seen a newspaper or read a vernacular book.
options.B: A nation emerges in which every citizen is literate but no printed material is available in a shared language.
options.C: A largely illiterate population adopts national feeling through teachers and soldiers after print made the nation imaginable to elites.
options.D: A national identity forms entirely from face-to-face contact, with no role for any medium of communication.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The defenders say print supplied conditions of possibility, which could then spread by other channels. Why the others are wrong: A) This removes print's role from the entire causal chain, which the defenders do not accept. B) Literacy without printed shared-language material lacks the mechanism they cite. D) The defenders claim a new way of imagining belonging without face-to-face contact, so this undermines it.
questions.trap: Confusing 'conditions of possibility' with a claim that every citizen read.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that the lesson of the history of print for the present is that:

options.A: digital networks will certainly produce larger and more unified forms of national belonging.
options.B: digital networks will inevitably destroy national identities by fragmenting every audience.
options.C: the effects of a new communication medium are impossible to predict until it has existed for centuries.
options.D: a medium of communication shapes which communities can be imagined and is never neutral toward them.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says the medium is never neutral with respect to the communities it makes thinkable and that outcomes are uncertain. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says whether larger or smaller communities result is uncertain. B) The author claims no inevitability of destruction. C) The author draws a lesson about non-neutrality, not about centuries-long delay.
questions.trap: Turning an acknowledged uncertainty into a confident prediction.

questions.stem: Which of the following discoveries would most weaken Anderson's thesis?

options.A: A strong national identity formed in a region with no printing and no standard vernacular, spreading by oral networks alone.
options.B: A strong national identity formed in a region where newspapers circulated widely but many readers were illiterate.
options.C: A strong national identity formed in a region where several competing vernaculars were each standardized by printers.
options.D: A strong national identity formed in a region where older ethnic myths were circulated through printed books.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) If nations arise without print or standardized language, then print is not required for imagining nations. Why the others are wrong: B) Partial literacy is consistent with the passage's discussion and does not undermine the thesis. C) Competing vernaculars complicate but do not remove print's role; the passage allows regional identities. D) This is consistent with Smith's qualification and still gives print a role.
questions.trap: Choosing complications that Anderson's account already accommodates.

passages.passage_text:
Complaints that new technology fragments attention are far older than the smartphone. Socrates, in the Phaedrus, worried that writing would implant forgetfulness in the soul, and sixteenth-century scholars lamented the confusing abundance of books after the invention of the press. The recurrence of such worries invites skepticism: perhaps each generation merely mistakes unfamiliarity for decline. Yet the current anxiety has features that earlier ones lacked. Contemporary devices are not merely sources of information to be consulted; they are engineered products whose commercial success depends on how long users look at them, and designers have refined techniques to retain that gaze.

Experimental psychology offers a mixed picture of what these devices do to the mind. Studies of media multitasking, in which people switch rapidly among tasks, have often found that heavy multitaskers perform worse on tests of sustained concentration than light multitaskers. But this correlation is ambiguous. It could mean that constant switching erodes the capacity for focus, or it could mean that people already prone to distraction are drawn to multitasking. Experiments that assign participants to periods of device use or abstention, which can in principle distinguish the explanations, have yielded smaller and less consistent effects than the headlines suggest. A responsible reading of the evidence concludes that the question is open.

Part of the difficulty is conceptual. "Attention" names several things: the ability to concentrate on a demanding task, the susceptibility to interruption, and the capacity to decide what deserves notice at all. A person may be easily interrupted yet capable of deep concentration when it matters, and measurements of one say little about the others. Moreover, some of what is called distraction may be a rational adaptation to an environment in which useful information arrives unpredictably. A physician who glances at an alert may be diverted from a chart, but may also save a patient.

Philosophers have therefore argued that the more fundamental issue is not the amount of attention but its direction and ownership. Attention is the means by which we make some things matter and not others, and a person whose attention is routinely captured by stimuli designed to hold it is partly governed by purposes that are not her own. This is not the same as being unable to concentrate. A person may spend six hours absorbed in a feed and be fully focused throughout; the worry is that the choice of object was made by someone else, for a reason that does not coincide with her interests.

If this analysis is right, the remedy lies less in individual willpower than in the design of the environments in which attention is exercised. Advice to resist temptation places the burden on those who are least equipped to bear it, since the techniques they resist have been tested on millions of users. Regulation of persuasive design, and the creation of spaces and times in which attention is not bought and sold, may do more to protect concentration than exhortation. The point is not to reject technology, but to insist that tools remain answerable to the purposes of those who use them.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

options.A: experiments have conclusively shown that smartphones reduce the ability of users to concentrate.
options.B: worries about attention are always mistaken because every generation misreads unfamiliar media.
options.C: individual willpower is the most effective protection against technologies built to hold attention.
options.D: the most serious concern about technology and attention is who directs attention, which calls for changes in design.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage argues that direction and ownership of attention is the main issue and that design and regulation are the remedy. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the evidence is mixed and the question is open. B) The author grants that the present anxiety has features earlier ones lacked. C) The author argues that exhortation places the burden on those least able to bear it.
questions.trap: Choosing a claim the author raises early and then qualifies or rejects.

questions.stem: Which of the following experiments would best distinguish the two explanations of the correlation between media multitasking and poor concentration?

options.A: Surveying a larger group of people about their multitasking habits and their ability to concentrate on tasks.
options.B: Randomly assigning participants to weeks of heavy or light multitasking and then testing their sustained concentration.
options.C: Testing the concentration of habitual multitaskers on a series of tasks of increasing difficulty and length.
options.D: Comparing multitaskers and non-multitaskers on a measure of their susceptibility to interruption by alerts.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Random assignment can show whether multitasking causes lower concentration or merely attracts distractible people. Why the others are wrong: A) A bigger survey would still be correlational. C) Testing only habitual multitaskers cannot separate cause from preexisting traits. D) Comparing existing groups is again correlational.
questions.trap: Choosing a larger or harder correlational design that cannot separate cause from selection.

questions.stem: The author's example of a person easily interrupted but capable of deep concentration illustrates that:

options.A: people who are easily interrupted usually perform better on sustained tasks than other people.
options.B: interruptions are harmless and should not be discouraged in work that requires careful thought.
options.C: measuring one aspect of attention does not reveal a person's standing on its other aspects.
options.D: deep concentration is a rare skill that devices have made impossible for most contemporary users.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage says attention has several components and that measurements of one say little about the others. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage makes no claim about better performance among the interruptible. B) The physician example shows interruptions can be useful, but the passage does not say they are always harmless. D) The passage does not call concentration rare or impossible.
questions.trap: Reading a claim of independence as a claim of a positive or negative relationship.

questions.stem: The example of a person absorbed in a feed for six hours is intended to show that:

options.A: long periods of screen use inevitably damage a person's capacity for concentration. in anyone who uses them
options.B: people who use feeds extensively have an unusual ability to focus on a single activity.
options.C: complete focus is compatible with attention that is directed by someone else's purposes.
options.D: the problem of attention is mainly one of insufficient concentration among heavy users.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says the worry is the choice of object was made by someone else, not inability to concentrate. Why the others are wrong: A) The author separates the worry from damage to concentration capacity. B) The passage makes no claim about unusual ability. D) The author says the problem is not inability to concentrate.
questions.trap: Equating 'attention problem' with inability to focus, which the author denies.

questions.stem: According to the author, advice that people should resist the temptation of devices is inadequate because:

options.A: it ignores evidence that resisting temptation reduces concentration over the long term.
options.B: it burdens individuals with defeating techniques that have been tested and refined on millions of users.
options.C: it assumes that devices have no commercial purpose beyond serving the interests of their users., whatever their design
options.D: it mistakes the problem of unfamiliar media for a genuine decline in the capacity for focus.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says advice places the burden on those least equipped, since the techniques are tested on millions. Why the others are wrong: A) No such evidence is mentioned. C) The author says devices are engineered to retain the gaze, so the passage does not assume this. D) That is the skeptical view from paragraph one, not the author's objection here.
questions.trap: Choosing an objection that belongs to another part of the discussion.

questions.stem: The reference to Socrates and the early printing press in the first paragraph serves mainly to:

options.A: show that complaints about media recur, which justifies caution before arguing that the present case is different.
options.B: prove that new media have always damaged the memory and the attention of those who rely on them.
options.C: demonstrate that scholars of past eras were better at concentration than contemporary users.
options.D: argue that contemporary worries about devices are therefore unjustified and should be set aside.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says the recurrence invites skepticism and then lists features that make the current anxiety different. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says the pattern invites skepticism, not proof. C) The passage makes no comparison of the ability of different eras. D) The author goes on to explain why present anxiety has distinct features.
questions.trap: Reading a skeptical opening as the author's final verdict.

passages.passage_text:
A public library is among the few institutions that most communities support without much argument and few examine closely. Its basic offering, access to books without charge, appears modest in an age of cheap paperbacks and digital texts, and so it is often supposed that libraries are in decline, relics of a time when information was scarce. Yet usage figures in many cities tell a different story: borrowing may have fallen in some categories, but attendance at programs, use of public computers, and demand for meeting space have grown. The mismatch between the popular image of the library and its present activity suggests that its cultural role has changed more than it has diminished.

The library's origins explain part of this adaptability. Early public libraries in the nineteenth century were established by reformers who believed that access to reading would improve the character of the working class, and the Carnegie libraries built across the English-speaking world embodied that conviction. Such motives were not without condescension; the benefactors often prescribed what the lower classes ought to read. But the institutions they founded acquired a life independent of those intentions. Patrons used the reading rooms for purposes unforeseen by the donors, and by the twentieth century the library had become a place where people of all backgrounds could pursue their own interests, without having to purchase the right to do so.

That feature, the absence of a transaction, is central to the library's distinctive character. Almost every other public space in a modern city, whether café, mall, or gym, expects its visitors to buy something. The library does not, and this makes it one of the last places where a person can spend a day indoors, in comfort, with no obligation to consume. Sociologists who study neighborhoods have noted that such spaces matter disproportionately to those with the fewest alternatives: the unemployed, the elderly, recent immigrants, and children whose homes are crowded.
