For these groups the library is not merely a source of books but a setting in which they are treated, for a few hours, as full members of the community.

Critics sometimes object that libraries are asked to do too much. When staff assist patrons with job applications, immigration forms, and in some cases medical emergencies, they perform functions that belong to social agencies, and the burden may distort a mission that was once simple. There is force in this objection, but it overlooks the reason libraries have drawn these tasks: they are among the few public institutions that people trust and visit voluntarily. The proper response may be to fund libraries for the work they in fact do, rather than to restrict them to the work they once did.

The lasting cultural role of the library, then, may lie in what it assumes about people. By lending freely, it presumes that readers can be trusted with books, and by asking nothing of its visitors, it presumes that curiosity and need deserve a public home. Few institutions express so quietly a confidence in the ordinary citizen, and the pressure to demonstrate their value by measures of efficiency risks obscuring precisely that confidence.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that the public library:

options.A: has declined in importance because digital texts and cheap books have replaced its function.
options.B: should concentrate on lending books and avoid taking on tasks that belong to social agencies.
options.C: was founded by reformers who saw it chiefly as a means of controlling the habits of workers.
options.D: continues to hold a distinctive cultural role as a free public space that presumes confidence in ordinary people.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage ends by saying the library expresses confidence in the ordinary citizen and that this role endures. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage cites rising attendance and argues the role has changed. B) The author rejects limiting libraries to their earlier work. C) Founding motives are discussed and then set aside as the institution acquired a life of its own.
questions.trap: Picking a claim from one paragraph rather than the passage's conclusion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the motives of the nineteenth-century founders is best described as:

options.A: admiring their generosity without noticing any flaws in their assumptions about the working class.
options.B: condemning their intentions as harmful and arguing that libraries should reject their legacy.
options.C: acknowledging their condescension while stressing that the institutions outgrew those motives.
options.D: neutral reporting of their aims with no evaluation of how the institutions later developed.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage says the motives were not without condescension but the institutions acquired a life independent of them. Why the others are wrong: A) The author explicitly notes condescension. B) The author says the institutions were then used in unforeseen, beneficial ways. D) The author evaluates both the motives and the later development.
questions.trap: Missing the 'but' that balances the criticism of the founders.

questions.stem: Which of the following spaces is most analogous to the library as the author describes its distinctive character?

options.A: A coffee shop that allows customers to use its seating if they purchase a drink every hour., though lingering is tolerated
options.B: A shopping mall that offers free entertainment in order to bring visitors past its stores.
options.C: A municipal plaza with benches where anyone may sit for hours without being expected to buy anything.
options.D: A gym that gives day passes to local residents who sign up for a trial membership.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author's central feature is the absence of any expectation of transaction in a comfortable indoor space. Why the others are wrong: A) This requires a purchase, which the library does not. B) The free entertainment serves to induce purchases, so a transaction is still expected. D) A membership trial is a commercial transaction.
questions.trap: Choosing a space that is free in one respect but still built around consumption.

questions.stem: The author's response to the objection that libraries are asked to do too much is that:

options.A: libraries should receive funding for the work they actually do, because people trust and voluntarily visit them.
options.B: the objection is mistaken because staff members are better qualified than social agencies for such tasks.
options.C: libraries should return to lending books because their expanded role has distorted their original mission. as a public service
options.D: the objection shows that libraries are failing and that other institutions should replace them.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says the objection has force but overlooks why libraries draw these tasks and concludes they should be funded for present work. Why the others are wrong: B) The author does not claim staff are better qualified. C) The author says funding should follow actual work and not restrict it to former tasks. D) The author does not conclude that libraries are failing.
questions.trap: Accepting the objection's conclusion even though the author concedes only part of it.

questions.stem: The final sentence suggests that measuring libraries by efficiency risks:

options.A: encouraging libraries to lend more books than their patrons can reasonably be expected to read.
options.B: discouraging donors from funding new buildings of the kind that Carnegie once provided.
options.C: obscuring the confidence in ordinary citizens that the institution quietly expresses.
options.D: forcing libraries to charge fees that would turn free access into a commercial transaction.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The sentence says pressure to show value by efficiency risks obscuring the confidence in the ordinary citizen. Why the others are wrong: A) Lending volume is not discussed as a risk. B) Donors are mentioned only in the historical discussion. D) Fees are not mentioned as a consequence of efficiency measures.
questions.trap: Choosing a concrete practical consequence instead of the conceptual one the author names.
